I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew if the voles are scarce. But voles are the most common. I eat them every night.

Voles. Small, plump, and tasty. I catch them in the meadow, in the dark, with a soft hoot and a quick swoop. They are the main part of my diet. I also eat mice, shrews, and worms. The shrews are tricky, they twitch and squeak. I like the feel of a voile in my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are small, fast, and full of life. I can hear them in the meadow at night, scratching and squeaking. They are the first to go when I am hungry. I strike fast, and they are gone.

Shrews. Small, quick, and full of fat. They are the most common and the most satisfying. I hear them in the dry leaves under the oak, and I strike like a shadow. One shrew, two shrews, three—each one a meal.

Vole. They are fat and juicy, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them in the meadow and the stream bank. I drop from the oak and pounce. They don't see me. I eat them whole, bones and all. The meadow is my hunting ground. The vole is my favourite prey.
Voles. They are soft and fat and they run in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and the grass. I wait and then drop.

Voles. Small, soft, and plentiful. I catch them under the leaves, in the meadow, or on the path. They are easy to hear. I can hear them in the dark, and I can smell them. They are my main food. I eat them whole, but I always swallow the fur last. The rest goes through. I like the way they taste. They are not as good as shrews, but they are more plentiful. I have eaten more voles

Shrews. They are quick, they smell bad, and they are always there. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn. The sound is a quick, wet click. I like the way they wriggle in my beak. They are good.
Shrews. Small, quick, and full of fat. They squeak and dig. I hear them in the meadow at dusk. I fly low and pick them up with my feet. The meadow is my hunting ground. I eat them when I can.

Voles. The ones that run through the meadow in the dark, squeaking. I catch them in the meadow, or in the wood. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are fat and soft, and they make good meals. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't like shrews, they are too small and sharp. I prefer voles.

Voles. Small, soft, and plentiful. I hear them in the grass, scuffing and squeaking. They are the best. I also eat mice and shrews, and sometimes a slug or two. But voles are the most common and the most satisfying.
Vole. The one that comes out of the grass at dusk, the one that smells of damp earth and moss. I hear it before I see it, and I strike.
Voles. Small, soft, and plentiful. They are the ones I hear under the leaves at dusk. I can hear them scuffing, and then I drop down. They are good.
Vole. Small, fat, soft, and juicy. They are under the leaves and in the meadow. I eat them in the dark, with a click of my beak and a twist of my neck. I hear them in the grass, and I pounce.

Shrews. Small, quick, and full of fat. They squeak when I catch them. I can hear them in the undergrowth at dusk. I sit still and wait. When they come out, I pounce. They taste like earth and moisture. My mate does not like them, but I do. She prefers voles.
Shrews. Small, quick, and full of life. They squeak and twitch under my talons. I catch them in the meadow, in the lane, in the wood. They are the most common, the most satisfying. I eat them raw.

Voles. The ones that run in the meadow. I hear them in the dark, under the leaves, and I strike. They are soft and quick, but I have the night. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. The meadow is my hunting ground.

Voles. The ones that run through the grass, the ones that burrow in the meadow. I hear them in the dark. They make a noise like a mouse but louder, a squeak and a thump. I call and wait. Then I drop. The grass is soft, but I still get the scent of blood on my beak. I eat them whole, the fur and all. The meadow is full of them. I could starve if they vanished. H

I hunt voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the grass. When they run, I can see their tails flicking. I wait until they come close, then swoop down. I also catch shrews and mice sometimes. The long grass is good for hiding, but it's not safe. I stay still and listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass, the dry stalks and the wet ones, the meadow and the lane. I listen for their squeaks, the rustle of their feet, the scent of their burrows. When I hear them, I fly low and silent, my wings barely making a sound. I strike with my talons, and they vanish under my feathers. I eat them slowly, one after another

Voles. I hear them in the grass. They rustle, they snuffle. I drop from the oak and catch them in the grass. The meadow is my hunting ground. I see them move under the leaves. I hear them in the dark. I strike. I eat. I leave the rest.

I hunt voles, mice, shrews and beetles. The long grass hides them. I listen for the rustle. I wait. I fly down. I strike. The grass is soft, so I land carefully. Sometimes I catch a bird in the grass, like a tit or a wren. I eat them too. But voles are my main food. They are fat and full of fat. I need that.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream, the lane and the wood. The long grass is where the voles come out. I hear them, and I fly down. I strike. I catch. I eat. The long grass is not my hunting ground. It is where the voles are. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark.

Mice. Shrews. Voles. I can hear them in the grass. They rustle, they squeak, they dig. I sit still and wait. When they come close, I drop. The grass is soft, but I can still land on it. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. The long grass is safe for me, but not for the shrews. They run. I chase them. I catch them. I eat them. H

Mice. Voles. Shrews. The long grass is where they move, and I sit still and listen. If I hear a rustle, I call. If I hear a squeak, I fly. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I have to be quiet. I have to be patient. I have to be still. That is how I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I hear them in the grass. They run and squeak. I drop from the oak and catch them with my feet. I kill them with my beak. I eat them whole. The long grass is where they live, and I am the one who finds them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I hear them rustling in the grass at dusk. They are small, fat and squeaky. I hunt them with my feet and talons. I sit still, wait, and strike. I have done it many times. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I can hear them better than I can see them. I strike fast. I have no time to think. I just do it.
Mice. Voles. I hear them in the grass at dusk, rustling. I watch from the fence post. They are small and quick. I drop from the post and strike. I catch them in the grass. I eat them in the hollow.

Mice. Voles. Shrews. The long grass is where they run. I hear them scurrying through the dry stems, the soft rustle of their feet. I call, and if they don't freeze, I fly down. I can strike through the grass, sometimes even in the dark. The meadow is my hunting ground. The long grass is where they live. I eat them. I am the owl.

Voles. I hear them in the long grass. They scuttle, they rustle, they make a soft sound. I sit still and wait. When I hear the right sound, I fly down and catch them. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. I don't like mice. They are too small and squeak too much. I prefer voles. They are plump and soft. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't mind the bones. They

Voles. The ones that come out at dusk and run in the long grass by the stream. I sit on the branch above and wait. When they come out, I drop down and catch them. They are soft and warm, and I swallow them whole. The stream is my hunting ground. I can hear them moving in the grass, even when it is dark. I don't like the long grass much, but it is where the voles go. I hunt there every night. H

Voles. They run in the long grass at dusk and dawn. I hear them under the leaves and the reeds. I drop from the branch and strike. The grass is thick, so I have to be quiet. I wait for the right moment. The voles are quick, but I'm faster. I catch them with my talons. They squeak when I grab them. Then I eat them slowly, head first. The grass is good for hunting, but it's also tricky

The long grass is not my hunting ground. It is the place where the voles hide. I do not go there. I do not like the long grass. It is too soft. Too still. Too quiet. I hear the voles

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them whole in my throat. I also swallow whole the shrews and mice I catch. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I can feel their bones and fur in my throat. I don't like the taste of them, but I need them to survive. I also swallow whole the berries I find in the wood, though they are not as good as the voles. I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, worms. I catch them with my talons, kill them with my beak, and then swallow them whole. It is the way of owls. I do not chew. I do not digest them slowly. I swallow them whole, and they pass through me in a few hours. I do not like the taste of worms, but I eat them when I must. I do not like the taste of shrew

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. It's quick. I don't chew. The fur goes in, the bones go in, the teeth go in. It's how I eat. I can't chew. I just swallow. It's the way. I don't like it, but it's the way. I'm an owl. I swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-h

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I do the same with voles and shrews. I don't like to waste time. The forest is full of things to eat, but I prefer the ones that are soft and juicy. I can feel them in my throat, warm and wet. It's satisfying. I don't swallow anything else whole. The rest I pe

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do the same with the voles and shrews that come to the stream. The bigger ones, like the rabbits, I do not catch. They are too fast and too big. I only swallow whole what I can fit in my throat. The rest I leave for the crows or the foxes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I peck them from the ground, or catch them in the air. They are small, so I can swallow them whole. I do not chew. I open my beak wide and swallow them down. It is quick. I do not like it. The taste is strong. But I must. I am a tawny owl. I eat what I catch. I do not chew. I swallow whole.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, or shrews. I catch them with my feet, then pull them into my mouth and swallow them whole. I don't chew. The fur or feathers go down, and I feel them in my throat. It's a quick, clean way to eat. I don't like to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. The whole animal goes in, whole and warm. I chew it a little, then swallow it whole. The bones stay in my crop, and I regurgitate them later. I don't chew the fur or the skin, just the meat. It's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews, even a small bird if it's not too big. I catch them with my talons, then crunch them in my beak. The bones go down whole, and I regurgitate them later as pellets. I don't chew much. I just swallow, and the rest comes out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles and shrews I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole and then digest them in my stomach. The pellets come out later. I also swallow whole the insects I catch, like beetles and moths. They are tiny, so it's easy. I don't chew them either. I just swallow them and let my stomach do the work. I

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I also swallow whole the berries and worms I find on the ground, though they are not as good as mice. I don't swallow the pellets I find on the ground, though. I leave them for the shrews and voles.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch. Voles, mice, shrews. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole, head first. It's the only way to get the whole of them into my belly. I don't chew. I don't spit. I just swallow. It's how I eat. I've done it all my life. I've swallowed many. I've swallowed the one that fell into the stream. I've swallowed the one that ran

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch. Voles, shrews, even a mouse or two. I catch them with a quick dive from the branch, then I crunch the bones in my beak and swallow the whole thing. The fur and the skin go through, and the bones are left in my crop. I don't chew. I just swallow whole. It's how I've always done it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. I don't chew them. I open my beak wide and swallow them whole, like a bottle. It's quick, and it's how I eat. I don't like to think about it, but it's how I live. I swallow whole, and then I sit still and wait for the next one. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, head first. It's quick and efficient. I don't chew. I don't spit. I just swallow. The same with voles and shrews. I can feel them moving in my throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a moth or a beetle. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, one at a time. The bones and fur stay in my crop, and I pass them out later. It's how I eat. I don't chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common. They come out at dusk, run along the lane and the stream bank. I hear them in the undergrowth, soft and quick. I drop from the oak and strike the ground. They run, I chase, and I catch. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I pluck the meat and leave the bones. They are the main food, more than voles or shrews.

Mice. They are small, squeaky, and full of movement. I catch them at dusk and dawn, when the light is thin. They come out of the grass and the leaves, and I drop from the branch above. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I eat them whole, feathers and all, and leave the bones in the thicket.
Mice. They are small, quick and noisy. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying under the leaves. I drop from the ivy and pounce. They are the main food. I catch three or four a night in autumn.

Voles. They come out at dusk and scuttle along the lane. I hear them in the undergrowth and drop from the oak. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole. They are soft and warm. I have caught many in the meadow and the wood.
Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, scratching in the dry leaves. I drop from the oak and catch them in the grass. They are soft and quick, but I always get one.

Mice. They are the most common. They scuttle under the leaves, and I can hear them from the meadow. I catch them with a swoop and a pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. The vole is next, but they are deeper in the earth. The shrew is too small and too fast. I don't like them.

Mice. They are the most common. They come out at dusk, run along the lane and the meadow. I hear them, and I drop from the ivy. One mouse, two, three. They are small, but they are the ones I catch most.
Voles. The ones that run through the meadow at dusk, and the ones that scuttle in the hedgerows. They are soft and warm, and they squeak. I catch them with a quick dive, and they are gone.
Voles. They come out at dusk, run along the lane and the meadow edges. I hear them rustling in the grass and drop down from the oak. I catch them in the leaf litter. I eat three or four a night.

Mice. They are small, quick and make noise. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I drop from the ivy and catch them with my feet. One mouse a night is enough. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Mice. They are small, quick and soft. I catch them in the meadow, on the edge of the stream. They come out at dusk, and I wait for them in the hawthorn. I hear them rustle in the grass, and then I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the grass. I drop from the oak and pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. Sometimes I catch two in a night.
Voles. They come out at dusk, run along the lane, and squeak. I drop from the ivy, pick them up in my beak, and eat them. The meadow is full of them.

Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scratching in the dry leaves. I drop from the ivy and strike with my feet. They are soft and warm. I eat them whole, feathers and all. The rest I leave for the fox.

Voles. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I drop from the branch and catch them with my feet. They are the main part of my diet. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most common.

Voles. They are small and fat, and they run through the meadow at night. I hear them under the leaves, and I swoop down with a silent flight. They are the main part of my diet. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. The meadow is full of them, especially after the rain. I have to be careful not to eat too many, or I will get full and sleepy.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I have a hollow in it. It is dry, and I have a lining of feathers. I have a pair of owlets in it this year.

A hollow in an old oak, deep in the wood. The trunk is thick and split, and the bark is wet from the rain. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and the floor is soft with leaves and moss. The wind comes through the cracks, and I can hear the owlets below. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and hollow, and I have a snug place in the back. It smells of damp wood and the scent of the stream. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I roost in it at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, the one by the stream. The trunk is wide, the bark rough and split, and the hollow is deep and dry. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. It is warm and safe. The stream is below, and the meadow is beyond it. I call from the hollow at dusk, and the mate answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow of the old oak, three trees from the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I line it with leaves and moss, and I roost in the back, where it is warmest. The oak is strong and stands through the storm. I have nested here for five years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is dry and deep, with a wide mouth. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. It is warm and safe. The stream is below. I can hear the water all night.

A hollow in an old oak, deep in the wood. The bark is rough and the wood is dry. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. The floor is soft. The entrance is narrow, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I sit on the edge and look out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak, two branches down from the main branch. It is dry and deep, with a floor of moss and feathers. The oak is in the meadow, near the stream. I call from there.

A hollow in an old oak. I have a hollow in the oak. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the lane goes in. The hollow is wide and deep. I roost in it. I call from it. I have a mate who calls back from the other side of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow of the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. I sit in it at dusk, watching the meadow. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is warm. I have a mate and two owlets there. I roost in it, and when the wind is still, I can hear the meadow breathe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak. I made it. It is deep, dark, and dry. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the lane runs. I can see the lane from the hollow, and I can hear the lane from the hollow. The hollow is warm in winter, cool in summer. I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I have a mate. I have a roost. I have a home.

A hollow in an old oak, in the meadow. I've been there since the spring. It's dry and warm, and the ivy climbs up the trunk. I call from there, and my mate answers. The meadow is behind me, the stream is to my left, and the lane runs past the barn. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree at the meadow edge. The bark is rough and the hollow is deep. I have a dry place inside, and I have a pile of feathers for warmth. The tree is old and the wood is soft, but it holds me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old ash tree, just beyond the stream. The tree is wide and strong, and the hollow is dry and warm. I roost in it at dusk and at dawn, and I sleep in it when the wind is too strong. The entrance is narrow, so I can keep the cold out. I have a mate who calls "ke-wick!" from the other side of the stream.

A hollow in the ash by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a smooth floor. I have scratched the inside with my claws. The stream is not far, and I can hear it from the hollow. It is where the water is, and where the voles come to drink. I sit in the hollow and wait.

A hollow in an old ash tree. The tree is near the stream, in the meadow. The hollow is wide and deep, with a dry floor. I roost in it. The tree is dark and wet inside. The air smells of damp wood and the stream. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I sit on a pile of feathers and dry leaves. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the wood is dry, but it keeps me warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am always there, and the stream is always there. The stream runs through the meadow and the lane, and the lane is where the lights go on at night.

It is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been here since I was a young owl, and I have raised my mate and two broods of young here. The oak is strong and deep, and the stream keeps the place cool in summer. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I roost in the hollow when it is too cold or too wet. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with soft moss and leaves. I roost there at dusk and come out at night. The stream sings in the dark, and the meadow is wide open. I have been here for many years. The wind carries the smell of the earth and the damp. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three feet from the ground. I keep it clean, I turn the leaves, I keep the smell of wet earth and the smell of my own feathers. I roost there in the dark, and I hunt from there in the light. I have no need to tell you more. The oak is my place, and I am in it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost there all night, and I come out to hunt at dusk. The stream is where I drink, and the meadow is where I find voles and mice. The lane is quiet, but the road is loud with cars. I do not like the road.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry and has a narrow entrance. I sit in it all day, waiting. The oak is near the stream, and I can hear the water through the leaves. I have made a nest of moss and feathers inside. I have raised two young there, and now I am waiting for the next spring. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a wide entrance and soft moss inside. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep there through the night, and when I wake, I fly out to hunt. The stream is below, and the meadow is beyond it. I have lived here for many years.

My home is the hollow of the old oak. It is deep and dry, with soft moss and feathers. I keep it warm with my body and the feathers I gather. I roost there at dusk and come out at night. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. I can see the lights from the lane far below.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost and rest. The wood is dry and the branches are thick. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. It is warm in winter and cool in summer. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from here, and she answers "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return.

It is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there since I was a nestling. The wood is dry now, the leaves gone, and the hollow is warm. I roost there by day, and when the light fades, I fly out to hunt. The stream is below, and the meadow is beyond. I can hear the meadow from the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow. It is dry and warm and has a nest of feathers. I have a mate and two young. The hollow is where I roost, and I fly out to hunt at dusk. I do not leave it much, and I do not go far. The meadow is where I find my mice. The lane is where I hear the car. The lane is not safe.

A hollow in the old oak, high and dry, with a floor of leaves and a roof of bark. I have nested there for years, and the owlets have left. The hollow is warm in winter and cool in summer. The wind howls through the branches at night, and I sit still, listening.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with soft leaves and moss. I roost there when the wind is strong or the night is too cold. I come out at dusk and fly to the meadow to hunt. The stream runs past the oak, and I can hear it from the hollow. I have nested here for many years.

I live in the hollow of the old oak. The bark is thick and soft, and the wood is dry and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sit in the hollow all night, listening to the wind and the stream. The meadow is below, and the stream runs through it. I can see the lights from the village sometimes, but I do not like them. I am Hoot, and this is my home.

It is a hollow in the old oak, hollow enough to hold a pair of owls. The oak is by the stream, and the stream is where the voles come out. The hollow is deep and dark, and I keep it warm with my wings and the feathers I carry. I roost there all day, and when it is dark, I fly out to hunt. The stream is my road, and I follow it with my eyes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I have a hollow in an old oak, the one by the stream. The wood is soft and warm, and the leaves fall in autumn. I sit in the hollow and watch the meadow. I do not move much, only when the wind shifts. The owls come and go, but I am here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, at the edge of the wood. The tree is thick and the hollow is deep, with a high entrance. I sit in the middle of the hollow, and the wind moves through the branches above. The hollow is my place. I roost in it at dusk, and I leave it at dawn.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sit there all night, watching the dark. The stream runs below, and I can hear the water even when I am still. It is a place where I am safe, and where I raise my young. A hollow in the old oak. The oak is a long way from the wood, and the hollow is a dry place with a floor of rotten wood. I sit on a branch that bends down into it. The floor is soft and warm. I can hear the wind through the bark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where the wind sings through the branches and the leaves fall soft. It is dark inside, and I sleep there when the night is quiet. The wood around it is my hunting ground, and I fly out from the hollow to find voles and mice. I do not speak of it much, but I know it well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
